The Black redhorse (Moxostoma duquesnii) is a relatively large-bodied catostomid native to the Mississippi and Great Lakes basins. Field surveys indicate that sexually mature individuals sampled from the upper Mississippi River drainage reach a maximum recorded total length of 51 centimeters [Li = 51 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to older, slow-growing individuals. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capability in this species occurs at a considerably smaller body size, with the total length at puberty estimated at approximately 15 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15 centimeters]. This marked discrepancy between the size at first maturity and the asymptotic length reflects a life-history strategy common among iteroparous freshwater fishes, whereby early maturation allows individuals to contribute to the next generation before the risks associated with attaining a large body size are fully realized. Moxostoma duquesnii exhibits a continuous growth pattern typical of many cypriniforms, adding both length and mass steadily throughout its lifespan, although the rate of increment declines appreciably after the onset of gonadal activity. Recent work comparing growth trajectories among sympatric Moxostoma congeners has confirmed that the species maintains a moderately slow growth rate relative to its ultimate size, a pattern that may be linked to the energetic demands of its benthic feeding habit on soft-bodied macroinvertebrates.

Reproductive output in Black redhorse has been characterized through both field and laboratory investigations, with particular attention paid to the thermal conditions that govern oocyte development and spawning. Gravid females captured during spring spawning runs and maintained in controlled laboratory conditions at a water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] exhibited a maximum spawning rate of approximately 2.05 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.05 spawning events per year]. Given that each spawning event typically yields between 360 and 390 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 360 and 390 eggs per clutch], this reproductive frequency translates into a substantial annual fecundity that is consistent with the reproductive strategy of a moderately fecund, iteroparous riverine catostomid. The choice of a 14 °C [T = 14 °C] holding temperature during these experiments was deliberate, as it approximates the thermal regime that gravid Moxostoma duquesnii encounter during their spring spawning migrations when water temperatures rise across the lower reaches of tributary streams. The kap value of 0.85, which is within the range documented for other Moxostoma species, suggests a consistent allocation strategy across the genus. Observations of repeated spawning by individual females within a single season have been reported, confirming that the species is capable of multiple clutches annually under favorable thermal and hydrological conditions.

Hatchling size in Moxostoma duquesnii is directly related to egg diameter, which ranges from 2.6 to 2.9 millimeters based on previously published descriptions of fertilized ova. Using the geometric relationship for a sphere, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.144 grams [Wwb = 0.144 grams], a modest initial mass that characterizes the yolk-sac larval stage. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are highly endotrophic and rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-hatching, remaining in the interstices of gravel riffles before the yolk is fully resorbed. This small birth mass influences the early life-history trajectory, as larvae must quickly transition to exogenous feeding on microcrustaceans and rotifers to sustain subsequent growth. The energetic constraints imposed by such a limited initial energy store are considerable, and mortality during the yolk-sac larval phase is likely elevated in years when prey availability is low or when temperature regimes accelerate yolk depletion rates. Comparative data from other large-bodied Moxostoma species indicate that a neonatal mass of roughly 0.14 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.14 grams] is common among members of the subgenus Moxostoma, reflecting a conserved pattern of maternal investment in egg size and larval provisioning across this clade of benthic catostomids.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult Black redhorse has been estimated from length-weight relationships derived from extensive field sampling across the species' range. Based on the length-weight regression W = 0.01175 * L^2.97, an individual attaining the maximum total length of 51 centimeters [Li = 51 centimeters] would be expected to reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1,390 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,390 grams]. This is a substantial mass for a catostomid of moderate body size and places Moxostoma duquesnii among the heavier-bodied members of its genus in the Mississippi River watershed. In comparison, the wet weight at puberty, calculated using the same length-weight relationship applied to the total length of 15 centimeters at sexual maturation, is 36.6 grams [Wwp = 36.6 grams]. The ratio of the mass at puberty to the ultimate mass is approximately 0.026, indicating that individuals begin allocating resources toward gonad development at a relatively small fraction of their eventual adult body size. This pattern is consistent with a life-history strategy in which early reproduction is favored despite the energetic trade-offs that may arise from diverting resources away from somatic growth, a common feature among catostomid fishes inhabiting variable riverine environments where recruitment success is unpredictable across years.

Longevity data for Moxostoma duquesnii, compiled from otolith-based age estimates collected during population assessments in Wisconsin and Minnesota, indicate that individuals can reach a maximum age of 16 years [am = 16 years] under field conditions at a mean annual water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This lifespan is moderate among North American catostomids; some larger congeners, such as Moxostoma macrolepidotum, have been reported to exceed 20 years, while smaller-bodied species may live only 8 to 10 years. The 16-year maximum lifespan (16 years) [am = 16 years] recorded for Black redhorse corresponds to an annual survival rate that likely supports the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy, allowing multiple spawning events over the course of an adult's lifetime at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Growth increments in otoliths from older individuals become increasingly narrow, reflecting a deceleration in somatic growth as fish approach their asymptotic length, and the oldest specimens frequently show significant resorption along the otolith margin, complicating age estimation. The thermal regime at which these fish were sampled, approximately 15 °C [T = 15 °C] over the growing season, is typical of warmwater streams in the upper Midwest. At colder northern latitudes, growth rates are slower and longevity may be extended, whereas in warmer southern populations, accelerated metabolic rates may shorten the maximum lifespan while increasing annual growth increments.
